cases.title: The ₹20cr shortfall
cases.question: You released a feature worth ₹100cr in scope. Due to an issue, ₹20cr of that fell through. Walk me through exactly what you do.

stages.question: First 60 minutes: what do you do and in what order?
considerations: Assess blast radius: is ₹20cr still leaking or already lost? Contain first.
Stand up a war-room + single owner; notify stakeholders with a facts-only update.
Decide rollback vs forward-fix based on reversibility and time-to-fix.
Preserve data/logs for root-cause before anything is overwritten.
stages.pushback: Engineering says a clean rollback will itself cost ₹5cr in downstream breakage. Now what?

stages.question: How do you find the root cause? Give me your structure.
considerations: Confirm it's real, not a reporting artifact (instrumentation check first).
Internal: recent launch/config, bug, infra failure, dependency change.
External: seasonality, a partner/PSP outage, market event.
Segment by geo/platform/cohort to localize the ₹20cr.
stages.pushback: The metric team says tracking looks fine and the money genuinely didn't convert. Where do you look next?

stages.question: What do you change so this never happens again?
considerations: Add a pre-launch guardrail/canary + kill-switch for high-scope releases.
Define a real-time guardrail metric with alerting thresholds.
Blameless post-mortem; convert learnings into launch-checklist gates.
Right-size rollout (phased %) for anything above a ₹-threshold.
stages.pushback: Leadership wants the feature re-shipped this week. How do you balance speed vs the safeguards you just described?

cases.title: Should Razorpay build its own UPI app?
cases.question: Your CEO asks you to evaluate whether Razorpay should build its own consumer UPI app. Give a recommendation.

stages.question: Before any recommendation — how do you frame the decision?
considerations: Clarify the strategic objective: consumer distribution? data? defensibility vs PhonePe/GPay?
Frame as build vs partner vs stay-B2B, not just yes/no.
Name constraints: NPCI/regulatory, 30% UPI market-share cap, CAC of a consumer app.
stages.pushback: The CEO says 'assume distribution isn't a problem'. Does your framing change?

stages.question: Walk the trade-offs. What are the 2–3 real options and their costs?
considerations: Build: huge CAC, brand shift B2B→B2C, years to scale, but owns consumer data + defensibility.
Partner/embed: faster, lower risk, but weaker moat.
Stay B2B and go deeper on merchant payments/credit where they already win.
Consumer UPI is near-zero-margin — monetization must come from adjacent products.
stages.pushback: PhonePe and GPay own ~85% share. What's your honest read on Razorpay's odds?

stages.question: Your recommendation in 3 sentences, plus the one metric that proves you right.
considerations: Take a clear stance (most defensible: don't build a standalone app; double down on merchant + embedded UPI).
State the leading metric (e.g., merchant UPI TPV / attach of credit) you'd watch.
Name the disconfirming signal that would reverse your call.
stages.pushback: If you're wrong and a competitor's consumer app starts eating your merchant relationships, what's your hedge?

cases.title: Payments for very busy people
cases.question: You're the PM of Payments at Google, tasked with building a product for very busy people. Design it.

stages.question: Clarify scope and pick the user. Who exactly is 'very busy'?
considerations: Clarify: platform, geography, B2C vs SMB, existing Google Pay footprint.
Pick one segment (e.g., time-poor working parents, or SMB owners) and their JTBD.
State the core need: reduce time/cognitive load per payment decision.
stages.pushback: Assume it's Indian SMB owners. Does your design change?

stages.question: What are the top pain points, and which one do you solve first?
considerations: Enumerate pains: repetitive bills, reconciliation, remembering due dates, context-switching.
Prioritize one (e.g., automated recurring + proactive nudges).
Say why that one first (frequency + defensible with Google's context signals).
stages.pushback: How is this meaningfully better than what PhonePe/GPay autopay already do?

stages.question: Your solution + the success metric and a guardrail.
considerations: Define MVP crisply (not the everything-app).
North Star: time saved / payments completed hands-off.
Guardrail: failed-payment rate, trust/opt-out rate, fraud on automation.
stages.pushback: Automation increases fraud/mistaken-payment risk. How do you keep trust?

rubric: Narrowed to a real user + JTBD

cases.title: Checkout lift, fraud spike
cases.question: A new instant-checkout feature increased conversion 10% but also increased fraud losses 25%. What do you do?

stages.question: How do you frame this trade-off and what data do you pull first?
considerations: Compute net: is the 10% conversion $ gain > the 25% fraud $ loss? Get absolute numbers.
Segment fraud: which cohorts/BINs/geos/amounts drive the 25%?
Separate first-party (friendly) fraud from third-party.
stages.pushback: Finance says net revenue is still up 4%. Does that mean you ship it as-is?

stages.question: What levers do you have, and which do you pull?
considerations: Risk-based step-up (3DS/OTP) only on high-risk segments — keep low-risk frictionless.
Tune rules/model thresholds for the offending cohorts.
Velocity/limits on the exact fraud pattern; manual-review queue for the gray zone.
stages.pushback: Adding step-up on high-risk cohorts drops their conversion. How do you decide the threshold?

stages.question: How do you validate and what do you commit to?
considerations: A/B the targeted-friction version vs control; measure net $ + auth rate + chargeback rate.
Set a guardrail auto-rollback if chargeback rate crosses X.
Recommend: keep the feature, add risk-based friction — quantify expected net.
stages.pushback: Chargebacks lag 30–60 days. How do you avoid declaring victory too early?

cases.title: The AI agents don't trust
cases.question: Your GenAI fraud-decisioning assistant shows 85% agreement with agents in shadow mode, but agents report low trust in its recommendations. Diagnose and fix.

stages.question: How do you diagnose the trust gap? 85% agreement sounds fine on paper.
considerations: Analyze the 15% disagreements: are they high-stakes cases? That's where trust breaks.
Is the rationale human-readable and specific, or generic? Trust needs explainability.
Are false-negatives (says approve, is fraud) concentrated? One bad miss kills trust.
stages.pushback: Agents say 'it's right most of the time but I can't tell WHEN it's wrong.' What does that tell you?

stages.question: What do you actually change in the product?
considerations: Surface calibrated confidence + the specific signals behind each call, not just a verdict.
Make it escalate/abstain on ambiguous cases rather than guess.
Track overrides and feed disagreements back into rules/prompt; show agents their feedback changed it.
stages.pushback: How would you measure whether trust actually improved, not just agreement?

stages.question: What's your launch gate before moving from shadow to assisted mode?
considerations: Set thresholds: false-negative rate < X%, agreement on high-value cases, agent-satisfaction score.
Human-in-the-loop preserved; no auto-approve/reject.
Staged rollout with override tracking + regression re-test after prompt changes.
stages.pushback: Compliance asks what happens the first time it confidently approves a big fraud. Your answer?

cases.title: BigBasket detractor NPS
cases.question: You're a PM at BigBasket. How would you improve the NPS of detractors who gave a bad rating for partly-delivered items — assuming the fulfilment process is already optimized?

stages.question: The process is already optimized — so where's the NPS lever? Frame it.
considerations: Reframe: you can't fix the partial-delivery event, so target expectation-setting + service recovery.
Segment detractors: which items, order values, frequencies drive the worst scores?
Name the JTBD: the customer wants predictability and to feel made-whole.
stages.pushback: Leadership says 'we already refund the missing item — what more do they want?'

stages.question: Give me 2–3 solutions and prioritize.
considerations: Proactive real-time notice + choice (substitute / refund / redeliver) before it's a surprise.
Instant, generous recovery (auto-credit + apology) on partial orders.
Let customers pre-set substitution preferences to avoid the miss entirely.
stages.pushback: Instant credits cost money on every partial order. How do you justify it?

stages.question: What metric proves it worked, and what's the guardrail?
considerations: Primary: detractor recovery rate / repeat-purchase of affected cohort.
Guardrail: credit cost per order, abuse rate on the recovery offer.
Measure via targeted A/B on the detractor cohort.
stages.pushback: Some users will game the auto-credit. How do you protect against abuse?

cases.title: The cheese-buying app
cases.question: Design an app to help people choose which cheese to buy at a grocery store. (Pure product design — zero relation to your background, on purpose.)

stages.question: Clarify and pick your user. Who's confused at the cheese aisle and why?
considerations: Segment: novice/overwhelmed shopper vs recipe-driven vs dietary-restricted vs gifting.
Pick one (e.g., the overwhelmed novice) and their JTBD: 'choose confidently in 30 seconds'.
Clarify context: in-store, time-pressured, phone in hand.
stages.pushback: Why the novice and not the foodie who'd actually pay for this?

stages.question: What's the core experience? Walk the key flow.
considerations: Input by use-case ('for a burger', 'for a cheese board') or scan the shelf.
Output: a ranked shortlist with why, price, and pairing.
Reduce to the fewest taps — they're standing in an aisle.
stages.pushback: Scanning shelves reliably is hard. What's your v1 if the scan doesn't work?

stages.question: Success metric + how you'd know people actually use it in-store.
considerations: North Star: successful in-store decisions (add-to-cart / purchase follow-through).
Guardrail: time-to-decision, repeat usage.
MVP: skip the fancy CV; start with a guided-question flow.
stages.pushback: How do you keep this from being a one-time-use novelty?

rubric: Designed for the real in-store context

cases.title: UPI app engagement dropped 40%
cases.question: User engagement dropped 40% after a UPI app update. Why, and what do you do?

stages.question: What do you clarify before investigating?
considerations: Define 'engagement': DAU? txns/user? session length? Which one dropped 40%?
Timing: exactly at the update, or gradual? Which user segments/OS versions?
Rule out an instrumentation/analytics break from the release first.
stages.pushback: Analytics confirms tracking is intact and it's a real 40% on transactions-per-user. Continue.

stages.question: Structure the causes — MECE.
considerations: Internal: a broken/slow flow in the update, new permission prompt, added step, crash on some OS.
External: a UPI outage, NPCI change, competitor promo, seasonality.
Segment by OS/app-version/region to localize.
stages.pushback: It's isolated to Android users on the newest app version. What's your leading hypothesis?

stages.question: Name the likely cause and your immediate action.
considerations: Likely: a regression in the payment flow for that Android build (crash / added friction).
Action: hotfix or roll back that build; add a canary + crash-rate alert.
Verify recovery on the affected cohort before closing.
stages.pushback: Rollback takes 24h to propagate. What do you do in the meantime?

cases.title: Estimate India's daily UPI volume
cases.question: Estimate the number of UPI transactions in India per day. Think out loud and structure it.

stages.question: State your approach and top-line assumptions.
considerations: Choose bottom-up: UPI users × transactions per user per day.
Anchor: ~350–400M UPI users in India.
Assume avg ~2–3 UPI txns/user/day across the active base (many small P2M payments).
stages.pushback: Is 'active users' the same as 'registered users'? Adjust.

stages.question: Do the math out loud.
considerations: ~350M active × ~2.5 txns/day ≈ ~875M/day → round to ~0.8–1B/day.
Layer: heavy users (merchants, gig workers) pull the average up.
Land on a range, not a false-precise number.
stages.pushback: Give me a single number you'd defend, and why.

stages.question: Sanity-check against something you know.
considerations: Cross-check vs monthly: ~0.9B/day ≈ ~27B/month — in the right order of magnitude for India UPI.
Call out the biggest source of error (active-user % and txns/user).
State confidence: right within ~2×, which is what estimation wants.
stages.pushback: If I told you the real number is ~2× yours, where's your estimate most likely wrong?

cases.title: Design a payments API
cases.question: Design a payments API. What makes it good to build on? (PM lens — the why and what, not the code.)

stages.question: Requirements first — functional and non-functional.
considerations: Functional: create charge, auth/capture, refund, idempotent retries, webhooks, dispute handling.
Non-functional: reliability (payments can't drop), low latency, PCI security, clear errors.
Name the developer as the primary 'user' — DX is the product.
stages.pushback: Which single non-functional requirement would you never trade off, and why?

stages.question: What makes this API genuinely good to build on?
considerations: Idempotency keys so retries never double-charge.
Predictable, well-documented errors; sensible defaults; hard-to-misuse design.
Webhooks for async state; sandbox + test cards; versioning that doesn't break integrators.
stages.pushback: A partner integrates it wrong and double-charges customers. Whose fault is it, and what do you change?

stages.question: How do you measure the API's success and health?
considerations: Health: success/auth rate, p99 latency, error rate by type.
Adoption: time-to-first-successful-charge, integration completion rate.
Trust: incidents, double-charge rate, support tickets per 1k integrations.
stages.pushback: Tie one of these metrics back to a real product decision you'd make from it.
